form: In Proceedings of ICSNL 61, Ella Hannon, Laura Griffin, Brent Hall, Bruce Oliver, Danica Reid, Julia Schillo, Lauren Schneider, Reed Steiner, and Bailey Trotter (eds.). Vancouver, BC: UBCWPL. Philology of Secwepemctsín: The Phonology of Studies on Shuswap* Ethan Pincott Simon Fraser University Abstract: In this paper, I examine the earliest monograph on Secwepemctsín, Studies on Shuswap (1925) by Father Le Jeune, to determine what the phonology of the language was like at that time and how it may have changed in the last hundred years. Taking a philological approach, I transcribe the words of the text, including those written in the Chinook Shorthand, and attempt to reconstruct their pronunciation based on Le Jeune’s orthographies. The results show that some important Secwepemctsín sound shifts had taken place by 1925, while others were still in progress. Keywords: Secwepemctsín, historical linguistics, phonology, orthography, wordlists, Chinook Shorthand

In this paper, I examine the materials contained in Father Le Jeune’s 1925 publication Studies on Shuswap. Although earlier records of the language exist, beginning with a wordlist from Alexander Mackenzie’s arrival in the territory in 1793 (Nater 2019), and including wordlists from Gibbs (1877), Tolmie (1877), place names and sporadic vocabulary from Dawson (1891), and various materials from Teit’s The Shuswap (1909), Studies represents the first monograph specifically on the language, and therefore is of great interest in analyzing how the language may have changed (or not) over the last hundred years. It is also of historical interest for Le Jeune’s use of the Chinook Shorthand system to write the language.

form: I began by transcribing all the words contained within, in both the Latin and Shorthand forms, along with Le Jeune’s translation, a phonetic reconstruction of the implied pronunciation, and the equivalent word and meaning in modern Secwepemctsín. This resulted in a corpus of over 1100 words. I then noted for each word whether it was identical in form and meaning to the modern language, if it differed in phonetics, morphology, or semantics, or if it was otherwise unattested in the language. This philological approach, the analysis of texts to better understand the history of the language, has been applied to Salish languages before, including Doak (1983) for nsyilxcən, Mattina and Taylor (1984) for Flathead, Nater (2019) for Secwepemctsín and Nuxalk, and Reisinger and Griffin (2022) for ʔayʔaǰuθəm, and remains an important avenue for future research into the development of the languages.

form: This paper is concerned specifically with what we can know about the phonology of the language in 1925 at the time of the writing of Studies. In order to understand the phonology, I first explain the orthographies used by Le Jeune to write the language. This is followed by a description of known Secwepemctsín sound shifts that are attested in the data. Then I examine certain archaic features of the phonology in Studies that are lacking in modern Secwepemctsín, as well as miscellaneous sound patterns that are more difficult to classify.

form: Secwepemctsín (Shuswap) is a language of the Interior Salish branch of the Salish family, most closely related to nɬeʔkepmxcín (Thompson), and more distantly to St’át’imcets (Lillooet). It is spoken across a vast region of south -central British Columbia. The western border runs along the Fraser River, from just north of Pavillion up to Soda Creek. From there, the northern borde r cuts east through the Cariboo Plateau to the Rocky Mountains near Jasper, with the eastern border along the mountains to Invermere. The southern border includes Splatsin, the Shuswap Lakes area, and the Thompson River along Kamloops to Cache Creek.

There are two main dialects of the language, Western and Eastern, with the border between them lying roughly between Kamloops and Chase. These differ from each other somewhat in phonology, grammar, and lexicon (Kuipers 1989:9). Within the Western dialect, there are minor phonetic and lexical differences between the northern and southern communities, as well as between Simpcw and the rest. The language probably has less than 50 fluent speakers remaining, although language revitalization efforts are underway, with a growing cohort of semi-speakers and learners.

Secwepemctsín phonology is typical of a Salish language, with 38 consonants but only 6 vowels. The consonant inventory includes uvulars, labialized dorsals, and glottalized stops and resonants. Consonant clusters are common and relatively unconstrained in terms of which consonants can be in contact.

form: Jean-Marie-Raphaël Le Jeune was a missionary of the Roman Catholic Oblates of Mary Immaculate. Born in Brittany in northwestern France, he travelled to British Columbia in 1879 to missionize to the Indigenous peoples there, alongside Bishop Durieu who had spent some time in the province already. On the voyage over, Durieu provided Le Jeune with an instruction manual in the Chinook Jargon, which he apparently took to immediately. He arrived in New Westminster and was soon assigned to begin missionary work among the people of the Fraser Canyon. At Yale, he befriended an nɬeʔképmx convert named Michel, and began learning the language, which he soon realized would be considerably more difficult than learning Chinook Jargon. He also studied with an elder named Mary Ta-hwi-nak at Spuzzum, with whom he spent much time learning words of the language and translating basic prayers and catechism. After spending the summer in the Fraser Canyon, Le Jeune was recalled to St. Mary’s Mission in Mission, where he spent two years, before being assigned to the St. Louis Mission in Kamloops, arriving on October 17, 1882. This would be his home for the remainder of his career.

Despite his prominent role in the missionary history of this part of the province and the linguistic relevance of his work, it has been difficult to find sources on his life.

form: Le Jeune continued his learning of Chinook Jargon and other Indigenous languages, believing that this was a necessary skill to fully understand and preach to the Indigenous peoples he was charged with. His linguistic ability was noted by his peers. Over his career, he compiled and edited prayers and catechism in at least eight languages: Secwepemctsín, Halq’eméylem, Sḵwx̱wú7mesh, sháshíshalh-em, ʔayʔajuθəm, St’át’imcets, nɬeʔkepmxcín, and nsyilxcn. He travelled widely on his missionary circuit, frequently visiting the Secwépemc reserves of Deadman’s Creek (Skeetchestn), Bonaparte (St̓uxwtéws), Chu Chua (Simpcw), and Adam’s Lake, as well as the nɬeʔképmx reserves of the Nicola Valley. In 1928, when he was over seventy years old, he travelled to thirty -two different missions. By all accounts, he was well respected by the Indigenous people he ministered to, as well as the growing settler population, and was known for his knowledge of Chinook Jargon, Secwepemctsín, and other Indigenous languages.

Le Jeune began publishing the Kamloops Wawa newspaper in May 1891, a newspaper written in Chinook Jargon, Shorthand, and English. Its circulation varied from one hundred copies at the beginning to over three thousand at its height. He continued its publication largely single-handedly for fourteen ye ars. As a newspaper, it contained typical reporting and advertisements, but also religious materials and reminiscences by Le Jeune. Although it was a struggle to get financing for the paper, Le Jeune did not press Indigenous subscribers for payment and instead mostly relied on white subscribers to keep it afloat.

Le Jeune retired in 1929 and left Kamloops before passing away at St. Mary’s Mission on November 21, 1930. Studies on Shuswap is an important linguistic legacy, but this legacy is marred by the cultural genocide and abuse of students that occurred at the Oblate-administered Kamloops Indian Residential School. Le Jeune himself was certainly not hostile to the use of Indigenous languages2, but it is difficult to separate the man from the system that inflicted so much harm on Indigenous peoples.

form: 2 An interesting anecdote is that Le Jeune once addressed two Indigenous boys in a local language, which they did not understand. He admonished them, saying “[y]ou leave it to me, a stranger in your country, to speak your own language which you do not know” (Guerney 1948:160).

The manuscript is thirty-two pages long, and begins with a guide to the Shorthand orthography, which is followed by a listing of articles and pronouns. Section I is a list of numerals, including reduplicated and suffixed forms for counting specific classes of objects. Section II is guide to verbs, broken down into conjugation patterns according to tense and aspect. Section III is labelled “A key to the most usual words of the Shuswap language, adapted from the key to the garden of the Greek roots”. This begins with thirteen paragraphs written only in shorthand. These are religious in nature, including a translation of Genesis:1. The remainder is difficult to parse, due to my own limitations in identifying some of the words used, but it includes basic Catholic theology, such as a description of the Trinity. This is followed by a translation/adaptation of Genesis:1 in Latin orthography, Shorthand, and an English translation, about three pages total. This is not a direct translation of Genesis:1, but instead serves as a wordlist of Secwepemctsín nouns according to the work of the six days. Following this are more classified wordlists of nouns, which total four pages. Section IV is a list of adjectives, totalling about a page and a half. Section V is a list of verbs, mostly given in 1st person singular form, totalling about three pages. Section VI is a list titled “Adverbs, etc.”, covering remaining lexical classes (adverbs, demon stratives, interrogatives, particles, etc.), about two and a half pages. Section VII is titled “Reproduction of a few lessons in Shuswap”; these are a combination of hymns, prayers, and grammatical forms, and basic sentences, often relating to Catholic teachings. At the end of this section, there is a supplementary wordlist, and more basic sentences. The book concludes with a declaration that similar studies on Thompson and Okanagan are in preparation, but these were apparently never completed before Le Jeune’s death. For the most part, these are presented in three columns: the first containing Le Jeune’s representation of Secwepemctsín in Latin orthography, the second containing Secwepemctsín represented in Chinook Shorthand, and the third an English definition. However, some entries contain only Shorthand and an English translation, and some just a word in Shorthand.

form: The representation of consonants in Studies is surprisingly functional for its time. Le Jeune usually, though not totally reliably, distinguishes velar from uvular stops. The uvulars are mainly represented as ⟨kr⟩, and it seems likely that the choice of ⟨r⟩ in this digraph was influenced by the presence of a uvular rhotic in his native French. Similarly, the pharyngeal approximant is usually spelled ⟨r⟩. He is also largely accurate in distinguishing the voiceless lateral fricative ll /ɬ/, which he writes ⟨lh, hl⟩, from the approximant l /l/.

form: Labialization of dorsals is also consistently written with a rounded vowel grapheme, usually ⟨w⟩ or ⟨o⟩, following the dorsal. In coda position, the rounded vowel may sometimes occur before the dorsal. In situations where schwa occurs adjacent to a rounded consonant, it is typically written ⟨w⟩, so for instance ⟨kwC⟩ can represent /kʷəC/ or /kʷuC/.

Despite these features, there are some significant deficiencies of Le Jeune’s system. Glottalization of obstruents and resonants is not indicated, with the notable exception of ⟨tl⟩ for the glottalized lateral affricate t̓ /t̓/, distinct from the plain stop t /t/. Glottal stop is usually not written, but in some very rare instances it is indicated with ⟨h⟩ or doubling of the vowel preceding the glottal stop.

form: The sibilants s ts ts̓ /s, c, c̓/ are the most difficult to interpret. In Secwepemctsín, they are subject to significant dialectal and idiolectal variation. The plain affricate ts /c/ is the most stable, being pronounced as postalveolar [č] across dialects and speakers. Despite this, it shows the most variation in terms of graphemes used to represent it. Those most commonly used by Le Jeune, ⟨sh j tj⟩, seem to reflect this postalveolar pronunciation, however some rarer graphemes, like ⟨s ts z⟩ instead suggest an alveolar pronunciation. Perhaps in Le Jeune’s time there was more variation in how this sound was pronounced, but this is highly speculative.

The fricative s /s/ and ejective affricate ts̓ /c̓/ vary between alveolar and postalveolar. In Southern dialects, the ejective affricate is consistently alveolar [c̓], while in Northern dialects, it is postalveolar [č̓]. The fricative is usually [s] in Southern dialects, while in Northern dialects it seems to vary more between [s] and [š]. Le Jeune’s grapheme choices of ⟨s, j, sh, z⟩ for the fricative suggest variation in how it was pronounced. The graphemes ⟨z, ts, tz, j⟩ for the ejective affricate, by contrast, suggest a primarily alveolar articulation. Regardless, there is considerable overlap in graphemes used to represent the sibilants, so it is generally only possible to identify which phoneme Le Jeune intended if the word is recognizable in the modern language.

The vowel graphemes in Le Jeune’s romanization also overlap significantly with each other. Schwa e /ə/ is typically ⟨i⟩, but it may be ⟨w, u, o⟩ if adjacent to a rounded consonant. At the ends of words, it is usually ⟨a⟩. Likewise, é /e/ is typically ⟨a⟩, but may be ⟨o⟩ adjacent to a rounded consonant. The front vowel i /i/ is written ⟨i, e⟩. Interestingly, u /u/ is usually ⟨w⟩, although other graphemes like ⟨o, oo, u⟩ are also used. The back vowels a /a/, written ⟨a,o⟩, and o /o/, written ⟨o⟩, are rare. Stress is usually indicated with a grave accent over the vowel, but it is often omitted.

form: The Chinook Shorthand, or Chinuk Pipa as it was called in Chinook Jargon, is a writing system developed by Le Jeune in 1890 from the Duployan shorthand originally developed for French by Father Émile Duployé (Gurney 1948:110-112). Consonants are written in straight lines, which are distinguished by length and direction/alignment of stroke, and arcs, which are distinguished by direction. Both may be modified with diacritics like dots to indicate different sounds. The shapes are somewhat phonemic, so that f or instance horizontal arcs represent sibilant consonants , while vertical arcs represent nasals. Vowels are circular and written with dots and lines inside to indicate a specific vowel or diphthong. Adjoining graphemes connect cursively within roughly syllabic units, although the common character {h} is written as a dot that does not connect. Unfortunately, due to technical limitations, I have not been able to reproduce the Shorthand graphemes here. Instead, I invite interested readers to consult Le Jeune’s Chinook Rudiments or the text of Studies on Shuswap itself for a sense of what the script looks like and how it works. Instead, I have romanized the Shorthand according to the system used by David Robertson (Robertson 2025) and presented those here in curly braces. Any errors in transcription are my own.

form: The overall patterns of phonemic representation in Le Jeune’s Latin orthography hold for his Shorthand orthography. There are two dedicated symbols for uvular stops, distinct from velar stops, although again not always distinguished. There are two symbols for the lateral fricative. Two symbols are used somewhat interchangeably for both the velar approximants and uvular approximants. Uvular and velar fricatives are represented by the same symbol {h}, while glottalized stops and resonants are not distinguished, again with the exception of t̓ /ƛ̓/. Glottal stop is not represented.

Rounding is somewhat more systematic in Shorthand than in Le Jeune’s Latin system. There are dedicated symbols for pseudo-diphthongs beginning and ending with {w} which are used when a labialized dorsal occurs before or after a vowel respectively. However, the more common representation of labialization in coda position is with one of the graphemes {u, o} following the dorsal.

In Shorthand, there are only four sibilant graphemes, romanized as {s, sh, c, ch}, resulting in less ambiguity. In general, the same patterns hold as in his Latin orthography: s /s/ is usually {sh} or {s}, ts /c/ is usually {sh} or {ch}, and ts̓ /c̓/ is usually {c} or {s}. Therefore, the Shorthand spelling is typically more useful for identifying the specific sibilant, and thus the word, that Le Jeune was writing.

Certain special graphemes/grapheme combinations occur for sound combinations. These include {yu} for iw /iw/ and yu /yu/, and {yuh} for icw /ixʷ/, as in {shhwiyuh} scwicw /sxʷíxʷ/ ‘yellow avalanche lily ’. Additionally, there is a character {x} of unclear phonetic nature (see Section 4 for discussion). Finally, there is also the very common initialism {TK}, representing the name Tqeltkúkwpi7 /tqəltkúkʷpiʔ/ ‘Creator, God’, which uses the graphemes for {t} and {k}, but crossed over each other rather than joined cursively.

Despite the defects mentioned, Le Jeune’s writing systems are practical and easy to interpret by anyone with some familiarity with the language and a bit of practice. The way the script breaks words up into syllabic units enables the rapid identification o f syllables and words, especially commonly used ones. For these reasons, it is easy to see how Indigenous peoples were able to quickly pick up the Shorthand and become literate in their languages in a short amount of time.

form: Secwepemctsín has a well-known sound law, where multiple ejectives are forbidden within a word (Kuipers 1974:23). This is a type of dissimilation, found in other Salish languages but most pervasive in Secwepemctsín, that has been called “Grassman’s law for Salish”, in reference to the famous Indo-European dissimilation of aspirates observed in languages like Greek and Sanskrit (Thompson and Thompson 1985). The sound law can be seen historically by comparing Secwepemctsín with its close relatives nɬeʔkepmxcín and St’át’imcets:

As shown by these cognates, the first of a sequence of ejectives within the stem, consisting of the root and any reduplicative morphemes 4, becomes deglottalized. This rule remains productive within the language today in reduplication patterns:

In Studies, there is clear evidence that this sound law was already in effect. However, it is only visible in cases where the alveolar lateral ejective affricate t̓ /ƛ̓/ is reduplicated. As shown in (2), lateral t̓ /ƛ̓/ becomes central t /t/ when deglottalization applies, and this difference in articulation is reflected in Le Jeune’s spellings of ⟨t⟩ {t} versus ⟨tl⟩ {tl}. Other ejective consonants are written indistinguishably from their plain counterparts by him. In the reduplicated plurals ‘eyes’ and ‘ears’, the stop in the reduplicant is written as ⟨t⟩ {t}, implying plain t /t/, while the stop in the root is written ⟨tl⟩ {tl}, implying ejective t̓ /ƛ̓/, exactly as expected:
4 Prefixes and suffixes with ejectives are outside of this domain and do not cause dissimilation.

Despite only being apparent in words with t̓ /ƛ̓/, it can be reasonably inferred that the same deglottalization applied to other ejective consonants in Le Jeune’s time. This is perhaps not surprising, since Thompson and Thompson (1985) show that similar, but less extensive, dissimilation processes occur in various Interior Salish languages, suggesting that some of these patterns may be quite old within the branch.

form: One archaism recorded in Studies is a tendency towards the preservation of phonetic features in unstressed syllables that have been lost in modern Secwepemctsín. The language as spoken today reduces all unstressed full vowels to schwa, and unstressed vowel -glide sequences to a vocalized glide. This interacts with the mobile stress system of the language, causing alternations between full vowels and schwa, and between vowel-glide sequences and vocalized glides.

form: The Secwepemctsín stress system is complex, and the full details are beyond the scope of this paper. Here I am applying the analysis of Hall et al. (2025) of stress in nɬeʔkepmxcín. Morphemes are classed into four categories: “strong”, which contain an underlying accented vowel, “ambivalent”, which contain an underlying full vowel that is unaccented, “weak”, which lack an underlying vowel 8, and “unstressable”, which are never stressed under any circumstances. Accompanying this is a hierarchy determining which morpheme hosts primary stress: strong suffix > strong root > ambivalent suffix > weak suffix > weak root > unstressable. form: With this brief description of stress out of the way, we can turn to unstressed syllable reduction. Some examples follow in (7). A strong morpheme will have its vowel reduced to schwa if unstressed (6a, 7a), while an ambivalent suffix has its vowel deleted entirely (6b, 7c). In both cases, if the reduced syllable has a coda glide, that glide becomes vocalized (7c,d). A weak morpheme with coda glide also surfaces with a vocalized glide when unstressed (7b).

8 I previously argued (Pincott 2025) that weak morphemes in Secwepemctsín contain underlying schwa, to account for certain predictable patterns in surface vowel quality and correspondences with other Northern Interior languages. I now believe that an under lyingly vowelless representation could account for the same data, as in closely related nɬeʔkepmxcín (Hall et al. 2025), with some minor modifications to explain some Secwepemctsín-specific patterns.

form: It is reasonable to assume that cases with a strong morpheme that undergo glide vocalization have an intermediate form with schwa (e.g., /xtéwméɬxʷ/ > /xtewméɬxʷ/ > /xtəwméɬxʷ/ > [xtuméɬxʷ]), which brings these forms in line with cases like /mút-emíʔ/ > [mətəmíʔ], rather than necessitating a special case of vowel deletion in unstressed vowel -glide sequences. This requires the assumption of a sound law /əy, əw/ > [i, u], which can be supported with two lines of argumentation. First, schwa -glide sequences [əy, əw] never surface in closed syllables in the language. Second, this simplifies the description of other morphophonological processes in the language. For instance, Kuipers uses two notations for “total reduplication”: C₁əC₂ if C₂ is an obstruent, and C₁C₂ if C₂ is a resonant, in order to account for the fact that C₂ glides surface as vocalized in reduplications. If we assume underlying /əy/ and /əw/ > [i] and [u], then both types can be analyzed simply as C₁əC₂.

It turns out that the hypothesis of intermediate /əy, əw/ has some support from the materials in Studies, where morphemes with underlying vowel -glide sequences preserve this structure even when unstressed; in other words, they do not surface with a vocalized glide.

Le Jeune’s spelling of ⟨aw⟩ {aw} is ambiguous, and could plausibly represent either [*ew] or [*əw]. It seems plausible to reconstruct the pronunciation [*əw], since there is less of a jump from this pronunciation to the modern pronunciation of [u], and this has the advantage of matching the modern underlying representation suggested above. This would imply that the reduction of unstressed vowels to schwa had already taken place by 1925. However, we also see several examples in Studies of an unstressed full vowel [*u] where modern Secwepemctsín has /ə/. There may be cases of unstressed [*i, e], however, these would not be visible in Le Jeune’s writing system, since his spellings of these phonemes overlap heavily with his spelling of schwa.

form: These forms would seem to suggest that reduction of unstressed vowels to schwa had not taken place by 1925, implying a pronunciation [*ew] for Le Jeune’s unstressed ⟨aw⟩ {aw}. One final piece of evidence is that the change /əy, əw/ > [i u] seems to have already been in effect, demonstrated by C₁əC₂ total reduplication.

Tentatively, I suggest that the coalescence of /əy, əw/ > [i u] occurred first, continuing to operate as a surface filter in the phonology of the language up until today, eliminating schwa-glide sequences in closed syllables whenever they would occur. The complete reduction of unstressed vowels to schwa would have taken place after 1925. The fact that Kuipers, who began working on the language in 1953, though more thoroughly from 1968 on, records only schwa in unstressed syllables is surprising, since 28 ye ars is a short time for such an extensive change to occur in the phonology of a language. Perhaps the change was already in progress in Le Jeune’s time, and proceeded unevenly through different lexical items and phonological environments. Some examples hint at this, but unambiguous cases are hard to find.

form: Despite these caveats, the overall picture from Studies is one of conservatism when it comes to unstressed syllables, with full vowels being preserved to a greater degree than in the modern language. The Secwepemctsín of Le Jeune’s day would have more resembled neighbouring and closely-related nɬeʔkepmxcín and St’át’imcets in this way, with complete vowel reduction being a later divergence.

form: A final archaism attested in the materials on Studies involves the voicing of fricatives in the determiner system. This Secwepemctsín sound shift has not been treated anywhere in the Salish literature, to my knowledge, but can be clearly seen by examining cognates. The initial phonemes /ɣ/ and /l/ in Secwepemctsín determiner bases regularly correspond to /x/ and /ɬ/ in other languages:

One such prefix in Secwepemctsín is t̓ek- /ƛ̓ək-/. Leaving aside the function of this and other prefixes for now, we can see that when combined with bases beginning with the approximants r /ɣ/ and l /l/, the initial consonant of the base appears as a voiceless fricative, c /x/ and ll /ɬ/ respectively:

form: The determiners in Studies show an interesting pattern compared to their forms in the modern language. Looking first at the articles re /ɣə/ and le /lə/, we see that they are consistently written in ways that imply a voiced pronunciation : ⟨i⟩ {i} for re /ɣə/, and ⟨l⟩ {l} for le /lə/. The spelling ⟨i⟩ {i} for re /ɣə/ is not unexpected, since this is one of the most common graphemes that Le Jeune uses for schwa. He may not have heard initial /ɣ/, which is again not surprising; in the southern part of the Western dialect, this article is reduced to [ə] except in the most careful speech. The spelling ⟨l⟩ {l} for le /lə/ is also expected; in the southern communities of the Western dialect, this article is consistently syllabic [l̩].

So far, the forms of the articles in Studies align closely with their pronunciation in the modern language. However, the demonstratives are written in ways that imply a more conservative pronunciation:

As discussed in section 3, the spelling {h} is consistently used for the voiceless dorsal fricatives /x/, /x̌/, and never for the voiced approximant /ɣ/, which is instead written {r} or {g}. The fact that the demonstratives in Studies are never written with either of these graphemes, but consistently have {h} strongly implies a voiceless fricative pronunciation at this time.

However, there is a catch. In certain occurences of demonstratives in shorthand, Le Jeune uses a symbol resembling a vertical tilde that Robertson transcribes as {x} (Robertson 2025), which I have maintained, e.g.: {nixi} nerí7 /nəɣíʔ/ “at this”. This grapheme is limited to a handful of instances of demonstratives and occurs nowhere else in the materials of Studies. In the guide to the phonetic alphabet at the beginning of the document, Le Jeune describes the sound represented by this grapheme as “between h & r” (1925:2). Since his ⟨h⟩ represents the dorsal fricatives /x/ and /x̌/, while his ⟨r⟩ represents the dorsal approximants /ɣ/ and /ʕ/, it is unclear what a sound “between” these would mean. Two possibilities come to mind: it could be that he was hearing a true voiced fricative, rather than the typical soft approximant pronunciation the sound has today, or, perhaps more likely, that this was his way of representing words that varied in pronunciation between /x/ and /ɣ/ from speaker to speaker, or potentially even in free variation. Either possibility suggests that this change of voiceless fri cative to voiced approximant in the determiner system was still in progress at the time that Studies was written.

form: The last two examples are notable, since we see other examples of the loss of syllabic nasals in the modern language. The Eastern dialect is well -known for the near total loss of nasals in this position, with different vowel qualities arising depending on the specific nasal lost and the place of articulation of the preceding consonant (Kuipers 1989:17; Schillo 2023). However, even in the Western dialect, we see nasals lost historically, or variation between words with or without a nasal.

Clearly, the trend towards syllabic nasal loss has been prevalent in the language for some time, reaching its culmination in the modern Eastern dialect. The fact that certain words in Studies preserve syllabic nasals that have since been lost shows that this sporadic change has been in progress until very recently.

These two words are interesting in that they display nasal loss in 1925, whereas the modern forms preserve the nasal, which is further evidence of the general instability of syllabic nasals in unstressed syllables. form: Father Le Jeune’s Studies on Shuswap is a fascinating document, as it is the only source that provides a comprehensive window into the language at such an early stage. In the grand picture of the history of Secwepemctsín, 1925 is not very long ago, but there is still much we can learn about the development of the language in studying the early texts we do have access to. Overall, the phon ological differences described above are rare: in the corpus of over 1100 words in Studies, I have labelled around 60 as having phonological differences from the modern language. Despite this, there is evidence of certain archaic features preserved in the language as recorded by Le Jeune that have been lost in the intervening hundred years . Perhaps more importantly, the language in Studies shows evi dence of phonological change in progress , particularly in the development of unstressed vowels, and fricatives in determiners. It may seem surprising that these changes spread so quickly throughout Secwepemctsín-speaking communities in the decade s before Kuipers began his work on the language, but in Le Jeune’s time, Secwepemctsín would have been the everyday language for thousands of Secwépemc. Living languages naturally change from one generation to the next, and it may be that one generation was all the time needed for these specific phonological changes to spread throughout the language. A useful direction for further research would be to compare th e materials of Studies to other early recordings of the language, many of which predate Le Jeune’s work by decades. This would help determine when some of these sound changes began to take effect, and how quickly they spread.

For space and time, I focused in this paper only on what I could glean from Studies about the phonology of Secwepemctsín. There are many other interesting questions that could be asked about what evidence the materials contain about morphological, lexical, and syntactic change . I hope to explore these aspects in future ICSNL proceedings.
